title: Data Analytics with Python & SQL
tagline: The analyst's workflow: SQL for the data, pandas thinking for the analysis, and a clear story at the end
summary: Learn how an analyst works from question to decision. You practise the SQL side live in your browser on a shop's users, events and orders: funnels, cohort retention, segmentation, deduplication and a growth report. The Python side (pandas, plotting, statistics, pipelines) is taught with annotated code, each idea paired with its SQL equivalent, for you to run in a free notebook such as Google Colab. Python does not run in this browser, so the labs use SQL and sorting activities, and the final project is a SQL report and a written memo.

modules.title: The analytics workflow and Python essentials
modules.summary: See how an analysis goes from a question to a decision, how SQL and Python share the work, and learn the small amount of Python every analyst needs.
modules.outcome: You can turn a vague request into an answerable question, describe the stages of an analysis, say what SQL does and what Python does, and read and write basic Python with lists, dictionaries, loops and functions.
modules.intro: Data analytics is not a tool, it is a way of working: start from a question, get the data, clean it, analyse it, and explain what you found so someone can act. SQL and Python are the two languages most analysts use for the middle of that journey. SQL fetches and summarises data where it is stored; Python (with the pandas library) reshapes, explores and models it. This course teaches both side by side, so each idea you learn in one helps you in the other. Be clear about one thing from the start: the SQL windows and labs here run in your browser, while the Python code is shown for you to run in a free notebook such as Google Colab, so nothing in the browser pretends to run Python.

topics.title: From question to decision: the analysis workflow
topics.html:
Good analysis follows a repeatable path. Skipping a step is the usual reason for wrong or useless results.

The four kinds of analysis
TypeAnswersExample
DescriptiveWhat happened?Orders fell 12% in March
DiagnosticWhy did it happen?The fall came from one lost customer
PredictiveWhat will happen?Next month's orders will be about 540 to 600
PrescriptiveWhat should we do?Contact the five similar customers this week

Most business work is descriptive and diagnostic. Prediction and prescription build on them, so if you cannot describe the past reliably, a model of the future will not help.

A good analysis question is

  • Tied to a decision: someone will do something differently because of the answer.
  • Specific: 'Which acquisition channel gives the most repeat buyers in the first 90 days?', not 'How are customers?'
  • Measurable with data you can get.
  • Bounded by time, place and population.
Worked example

Sharpening a request

A manager says: 'Can you look at why users are leaving?'

  1. Ask what decision depends on it: 'Do we fix onboarding or change pricing?'
  2. Define the terms: leaving means no activity for 30 days.
  3. State the question: 'Of users who signed up in January to March, what share was inactive after 30 days, and how does it differ by signup source?'

Answer. A vague request became a question with a metric, a period and a comparison, which can be answered with a query.

Watch out

Starting with the tool ('let's use machine learning') instead of the question is the most common beginner mistake. A clear question often needs only a group-by and a good chart.

Common mistakes

  • Jumping into the data without a question.
  • Defining a metric differently each time (what is an 'active user'?).
  • Skipping communication: a correct analysis nobody understands changes nothing.
Try it yourself: Rewrite 'Is our marketing working?' as an analysis question.

Model answer. For example: 'Did customers who joined from the March paid campaign order more in their first 60 days than organic joiners?'

Check what you just learned

1. Which question is best for analysis?
  • Is business good?
  • Can we use AI?
  • How are customers?
  • Which source gave the most repeat buyers in their first 90 days? (correct)

It is specific, measurable and bounded.

2. 'Why did orders fall in March?' is which kind of analysis?
  • Diagnostic (correct)
  • Descriptive
  • Predictive
  • Prescriptive

It asks for a cause.
keyPoints: Analysis runs ask, get, clean, analyse, communicate.
Descriptive and diagnostic questions come before predictive and prescriptive ones.
A good question is tied to a decision, specific, measurable and bounded.

topics.title: Your toolkit: SQL, Python, notebooks and how they fit
topics.html:
Analysts use a small set of tools, each for what it does best.

Who does what
ToolBest atTypical use
SQLSelecting, filtering, joining and summarising data inside a databasePull last quarter's orders, already grouped by month
Python with pandasReshaping, cleaning, exploring and modelling data in memoryFix messy columns, draw charts, run statistics
A notebook (Jupyter, Colab)Mixing code, results, charts and notes in one documentAn analysis you can read top to bottom and re-run
SpreadsheetsQuick looks and small dataCheck a number or share a table
BI tools (Power BI, Tableau)Interactive dashboards for othersA weekly KPI view

A common pattern: let the database do the heavy lifting, then finish in Python. If a table has 50 million rows, summarise it with SQL first (GROUP BY) and load only the result into pandas.

Watch out

The Python code in this course does not run in this browser. Copy it into a free notebook (Google Colab needs nothing installed) to try it. The SQL windows and the labs do run here.

Getting started with no installation

  • Open Google Colab (colab.research.google.com) and start a new notebook; pandas, numpy and matplotlib are already installed.
  • Upload a CSV with the file icon, or read one from a URL with pd.read_csv(url).
  • Run a cell with Shift+Enter. Cells run in order, and the notebook remembers variables between cells.
  • Or install Anaconda on your own computer for a local Jupyter.
Worked example

Where the work happens

You need average order value by city for 40 million orders.

  1. Doing it in pandas means loading 40 million rows into memory first: slow or impossible.
  2. Do it in SQL: SELECT city, AVG(amount) FROM orders GROUP BY city returns a handful of rows.
  3. Load that small result into pandas for charts and further analysis.

Answer. Move as little data as possible: filter and summarise near the data, then analyse the small result.

Tip

You do not have to choose between SQL and Python. The strongest analysts are fluent enough in both to move the work to wherever it is easiest.

Common mistakes

  • Pulling an entire table into Python when a query would do.
  • Writing analysis code with no notes, so no one (including you) can follow it later.
  • Running notebook cells out of order and getting results that cannot be reproduced.

Check what you just learned

1. What should you do before loading a 50-million-row table into pandas?
  • Load it all
  • Summarise or filter it with SQL first (correct)
  • Print it
  • Convert it to Excel

Move as little data as you can.

2. A notebook is useful because it:
  • Replaces SQL
  • Hides errors
  • Combines code, results and notes in one re-runnable document (correct)
  • Is a database

It is readable top to bottom and can be re-run.
keyPoints: SQL summarises where data lives; pandas reshapes and explores in memory; notebooks combine code, charts and notes.
Do the heavy filtering and grouping in SQL, then load the small result into pandas.
Google Colab runs Python with nothing installed.

topics.title: Python essentials for analysts
topics.html:
You need only a small slice of Python to be productive with pandas. Here it is.

Core types
TypeExampleNotes
int, float42, 3.14Whole and decimal numbers
str"Pune"Text, in quotes
boolTrue, FalseCapital first letter
list[10, 20, 30]Ordered, changeable; index from 0
dict{"city": "Pune", "n": 3}Key to value pairs
NoneNoneNo value (like SQL NULL)

Habits worth forming early

  • Indentation is syntax. The indented lines belong to the def, for or if above them.
  • Counting starts at 0. The first item is [0], the last is [-1].
  • = assigns, == compares. x = 5 stores; x == 5 asks.
  • Read the error from the bottom. The last line names the problem; the lines above show where.
  • Use meaningful names. monthly_revenue, not x2.
Worked example

A loop and what it replaces

Add 18% GST to each amount.

  1. With a loop: taxed = [], then for a in amounts: taxed.append(a * 1.18).
  2. With a comprehension: taxed = [a * 1.18 for a in amounts].
  3. In pandas you will not write either: df["amount"] * 1.18 applies to every row at once.

Answer. Loops are fine for small things, but pandas works on whole columns at a time ('vectorised'), which is shorter and far faster.

Watch out

Mixing tabs and spaces, or inconsistent indentation, gives an IndentationError. Let the notebook indent for you, and use four spaces.

Common mistakes

  • Writing = where == is needed inside an if.
  • Forgetting a colon after def, for, if or else.
  • Confusing [ ] (list or index), ( ) (call or tuple) and { } (dict).
Try it yourself: What does [x * 2 for x in [1, 2, 3] if x > 1] return?

Model answer. [4, 6]: it doubles only the values greater than 1.

Check what you just learned

1. In `amounts = [500, 300, 700]`, what is `amounts[0]`?
  • 300
  • 0
  • 700
  • 500 (correct)

Counting starts at 0, so index 0 is the first item.

2. What does `==` do?
  • Compares two values (correct)
  • Assigns a value
  • Adds
  • Deletes

`=` assigns; `==` compares.
keyPoints: Know int, float, str, bool, list, dict and None, and that counting starts at 0.
A function packages a calculation; an f-string builds text.
pandas works on whole columns at once, so you rarely need loops.

topics.title: Tables as objects: DataFrames and vectorised thinking
topics.html:
The main object in pandas is the DataFrame: a table with labelled columns and a row index, much like a SQL table or a spreadsheet range. A single column is a Series.

The same idea in three tools
ConceptSQLpandasSpreadsheet
A tableTableDataFrameA sheet range
One columnColumnSeriesA column
One rowRowA row of the DataFrameA row
The keyPrimary keyIndexRow number
Column typeColumn typedtypeNumber format

Vectorised thinking is the key mental shift. In SQL you write one expression and it applies to every row; pandas does the same on columns. df["amount"] * 1.18 multiplies the whole column, with no loop.

One expression, every row

The SQL equivalent of df["amount"] * 1.18: a calculated column. Change the rate or add another column.

Tables: orders. Starting query:

SELECT id, amount, ROUND(amount * 1.18, 0) AS with_gst
FROM orders
ORDER BY id
LIMIT 6;
Worked example

The same task three ways

Total revenue per city, largest first.

  1. SQL: SELECT city, SUM(amount) FROM t GROUP BY city ORDER BY 2 DESC.
  2. pandas: df.groupby("city")["amount"].sum().sort_values(ascending=False).
  3. Spreadsheet: a PivotTable with city in Rows and amount in Values.

Answer. Different syntax, identical logic. Learning to translate between them is a core skill, and this course practises it.

Watch out

A DataFrame copy is not always a copy. Changing a slice can raise a SettingWithCopyWarning. Make an explicit copy with .copy() when you plan to modify a subset.

Common mistakes

  • Writing loops over rows when a column expression would do.
  • Assuming the index is a row number. After filtering, it keeps the original labels.
  • Forgetting that df["a"] returns a Series and df[["a"]] returns a DataFrame.
Try it yourself: How many rows and columns does df.shape report for a table of 3 customers and 3 columns?

Model answer. (3, 3): the first number is rows, the second is columns.

Check what you just learned

1. What is a Series?
  • A whole table
  • One column of a DataFrame (correct)
  • A chart
  • A database

A Series is a single labelled column.

2. Why avoid row loops in pandas?
  • They are illegal
  • Loops delete data
  • Column operations are shorter and much faster (correct)
  • They need SQL

Vectorised code is the idiom.

Key terms: flip and sort

Workflow
Ask, get, clean, analyse, communicate.
Descriptive analysis
What happened.
DataFrame
A table of labelled columns in pandas.
Series
One column of a DataFrame.
Vectorised
Applied to a whole column at once.
Notebook
A document mixing code, results and notes.
dtype
The data type of a column.
keyPoints: A DataFrame is a table; one column is a Series; the index labels the rows.
Vectorised operations act on whole columns with no loop.

modules.title: Think in tables: select, filter, create and clean
modules.summary: Select columns and rows, filter with conditions, create and convert columns, and handle missing data and duplicates, in pandas and in its SQL equivalent.
modules.outcome: You can inspect a dataset, choose rows and columns, build conditions, create new columns, work with dates and text, and decide how to treat missing values and duplicates.
modules.intro: Most of an analyst's day is spent on four verbs: look, choose, create, clean. This module teaches each in pandas and shows the SQL that does the same job, so you can move between them. The labs practise the logic in SQL, which runs in your browser, because the idea (not the syntax) is the hard part.

topics.title: Looking at a dataset before you touch it
topics.html:
Before any analysis, look. Five quick commands tell you what you have.

What each tells you
CommandLooks for
head()Whether the columns and values look as you expect
shapeHow big the data is
info()Types (a date stored as text?) and missing values
describe()Odd minimums and maximums, skew (mean far from the 50% value)
value_counts()Typos in categories: 'Delhi' and 'delhi ' counted separately

The SQL equivalents are queries, and the practice window below holds the ShopLens users table. A profiling query answers 'how big is it, and what does it span?':

Profile a table with SQL

Size, date range and number of distinct sources, in one row. Add the count of free and pro plans.

Tables: users. Starting query:

SELECT COUNT(*) AS users,
       MIN(signup_date) AS first_signup,
       MAX(signup_date) AS last_signup,
       COUNT(DISTINCT source) AS sources
FROM users;
Worked example

A first look that saves a day

df.info() shows signup_date as object (text) and city with 33 non-null out of 36.

  1. object for a date means it is text: convert it with pd.to_datetime before doing date maths.
  2. 33 of 36 means three cities are missing: decide how to treat them.
  3. describe() showed a maximum order of 90,000 while the 75% value was 2,500: look at that row.

Answer. Three problems found in thirty seconds, before they could spoil a result.

Watch out

Never skip this step because the data 'comes from a trusted system'. Trusted systems still produce nulls, duplicates and test records.

Common mistakes

  • Analysing straight away without checking types.
  • Reading describe() without checking the count column for missing values.
  • Not looking at the actual rows, only the summaries.
Try it yourself: What does it mean when describe() shows a mean of 1,800 and a 50% value of 700?

Model answer. The distribution is skewed: a few large values pull the mean above the median. Look at the largest values.

Check what you just learned

1. Which command shows column types and non-null counts?
  • df.head()
  • df.sum()
  • df.shape
  • df.info() (correct)

info() lists each column's dtype and non-null count.

2. A date column showing as `object` means:
  • It is stored as text (correct)
  • It is perfect
  • It is empty
  • It is a number

Convert it with pd.to_datetime.
keyPoints: Start with head, shape, info, describe and value_counts.
Check types and missing values before analysing.
A profiling query gives the same first look in SQL.

topics.title: Selecting and filtering rows and columns
topics.html:
pandas gives several ways to choose data. Learn three and you can do almost everything.

Choosing data
GoalpandasSQL
One columndf["amount"]SELECT amount
Several columnsdf[["name", "amount"]]SELECT name, amount
Rows by conditiondf[df["amount"] > 500]WHERE amount > 500
Rows and columns by labeldf.loc[df["city"] == "Pune", ["name", "amount"]]SELECT name, amount ... WHERE city = 'Pune'
Rows by positiondf.iloc[0:5]LIMIT 5
Several valuesdf[df["city"].isin(["Pune", "Delhi"])]WHERE city IN ('Pune', 'Delhi')

The same filter in SQL

Pro users from ads or referral. Change the plan, or add a date condition.

Tables: users. Starting query:

SELECT id, signup_date, source
FROM users
WHERE plan = 'pro'
  AND source IN ('ads', 'referral')
ORDER BY signup_date;
Watch out

Use &, | and ~, not and, or and not, and put each condition in brackets. df[df.a > 1 & df.b == 2] fails because & binds tighter than the comparisons. Write df[(df.a > 1) & (df.b == 2)].

.loc selects by label and condition; .iloc by position. The two are easy to confuse: df.iloc[0:5] is five rows, while df.loc[0:5] is six rows because label slices include the end.

Worked example

Reading a filter in your head

df.loc[df["amount"] >= 500, ["name", "amount"]]

  1. df["amount"] >= 500 makes a column of True and False, one per row.
  2. .loc[mask, columns] keeps the rows where the mask is True.
  3. Only the name and amount columns are returned.

Answer. A filter is a True/False column used as a sieve. Debugging it is easy: print the mask.

Common mistakes

  • Missing brackets around conditions.
  • Using and / or, which raises 'truth value of a Series is ambiguous'.
  • Chaining df[...][...] = value to assign, which may change a copy rather than the original; use .loc.
Try it yourself: Write the pandas filter for users who signed up after 2025-03-01 and are on the free plan.

Model answer. df[(df["signup_date"] > "2025-03-01") & (df["plan"] == "free")]

Check what you just learned

1. Which combines two conditions in pandas?
  • a > 1 and b == 2
  • (a > 1) & (b == 2) (correct)
  • a > 1 && b == 2
  • a > 1, b == 2

Use & with brackets.

2. `df.iloc[0:5]` returns:
  • Six rows
  • Columns 0 to 5
  • Five rows by position (correct)
  • An error

iloc slices exclude the end.
keyPoints: Use df[cols] for columns, a Boolean mask for rows, .loc for both and .iloc for positions.
Combine conditions with &, | and ~, each in brackets.
Every pandas selection has a SQL counterpart.

topics.title: Creating and converting columns
topics.html:
New columns are how raw data becomes information: a total from price and quantity, a month from a date, a band from a number.

Tasks and tools
TaskpandasSQL
Arithmeticdf["a"] * df["b"]a * b
If-then labelsnp.where(cond, "x", "y") or pd.cutCASE WHEN ... END
Convert text to datepd.to_datetime(col)Cast, or ISO text with date functions
Date partscol.dt.month, .dt.yearMONTH(col), YEAR(col)
Clean textcol.str.strip().str.title()TRIM, UPPER, LOWER
Change typecol.astype("int64")CAST(col AS INTEGER)

A month and a band in SQL

The CASE does what pd.cut does. Change the thresholds and the month format.

Tables: orders. Starting query:

SELECT id, order_date,
       SUBSTR(order_date, 1, 7) AS month,
       amount,
       CASE WHEN amount >= 2000 THEN 'large'
            WHEN amount >= 800 THEN 'medium'
            ELSE 'small' END AS band
FROM orders
ORDER BY id
LIMIT 8;
Watch out

Apply is slow, and often unnecessary. df["a"].apply(lambda x: x * 2) works, but df["a"] * 2 is shorter and many times faster. Reach for apply only when no vectorised method exists.

Worked example

Date maths the safe way

An order_date column holds text like 2025-03-09.

  1. Convert once: df["order_date"] = pd.to_datetime(df["order_date"]).
  2. Now df["order_date"].dt.month and .dt.day_name() work.
  3. Subtracting dates gives a Timedelta: (today - df["order_date"]).dt.days.

Answer. Converting a date column right after loading removes a whole class of bugs.

Common mistakes

  • Doing date arithmetic on text, which silently compares as text.
  • Forgetting .dt before date parts.
  • Overwriting a raw column instead of making a new one.
Try it yourself: Which pandas call gives the month number of a datetime column d?

Model answer. d.dt.month

Check what you just learned

1. Which function turns text dates into real dates?
  • astype(int)
  • round
  • str.title
  • pd.to_datetime (correct)

to_datetime parses dates.

2. The SQL equivalent of pd.cut is:
  • CASE WHEN (correct)
  • JOIN
  • UNION
  • LIMIT

Both turn numbers into labelled bands.
keyPoints: Create columns with arithmetic, pd.cut, np.where and the .dt and .str accessors.
Convert dates once, right after loading.
Prefer vectorised code over apply.

topics.title: Missing data and duplicates
topics.html:
Real data has gaps and repeats. The skill is not the function that fixes them, it is deciding what the gap means.

What does a missing value mean?
CaseMeaningSensible treatment
Missing city on a signup formNot providedLabel it 'Unknown'; report how many
Missing discount on an orderProbably no discountFill with 0, after checking with the data owner
Missing amount on a purchaseA data errorInvestigate; do not guess; exclude and report
Missing age on a surveyRefused to answerLeave missing; do not average zeros in

Count the gaps in SQL

COUNT(*) counts rows; COUNT(city) skips the NULLs. The difference is the missing cities.

Tables: users. Starting query:

SELECT COUNT(*) AS users,
       COUNT(*) - COUNT(city) AS missing_city,
       ROUND(100.0 * (COUNT(*) - COUNT(city)) / COUNT(*), 1) AS pct_missing
FROM users;

Duplicates need a rule, too. Two identical event rows might be the same click logged twice (remove one), or two genuine events that happened at the same moment. Check how many there are, look at examples, decide what makes two rows 'the same', then remove with that rule written down.

Watch out

Dropping rows with any missing value (dropna() with no arguments) can delete most of your data when different columns are missing in different rows. Drop on specific columns that you truly need.

A missing-data routine

  • Count the missing values per column.
  • Ask why they are missing.
  • Choose: leave, label, fill with a justified value, or exclude.
  • Record how many rows each choice affects.
  • Check that the choice does not change the conclusion (try it with and without).

Common mistakes

  • Filling every gap with the mean without asking what the gap means.
  • Dropping duplicates by all columns when an id differs, so none are found.
  • Not recording what was changed.
Try it yourself: How would you count the missing values in each column of a DataFrame?

Model answer. df.isna().sum()

Check what you just learned

1. What does `df.isna().sum()` return?
  • The total of all numbers
  • The count of missing values per column (correct)
  • The number of rows
  • Duplicate rows

isna() flags missing; sum() counts them.

2. `dropna()` with no arguments can be dangerous because it:
  • Is slow
  • Fills with zero
  • Removes any row with a gap in any column (correct)
  • Sorts the data

You may lose most rows.

Key terms: flip and sort

info()
Shows column types and non-null counts.
Boolean mask
A column of True/False used to select rows.
.loc / .iloc
Selection by label or by position.
pd.to_datetime
Converts text to real dates.
Missing value
A gap: shown as NULL in SQL and as a missing marker in pandas.
Duplicate
A row repeating another by a defined rule.
keyPoints: Find gaps with isna().sum() (or COUNT(*) − COUNT(col) in SQL).
Decide what a gap means before choosing leave, label, fill or drop.
Define what makes two rows duplicates, then remove by that rule and record it.

modules.title: Group, join and reshape
modules.summary: Summarise by group, combine tables, reshape between wide and long, and compute running and rolling figures, in pandas and SQL.
modules.outcome: You can write groupby aggregations, merge tables with the right join and spot a fan-out, pivot and unpivot data, and use sort, rank, shift and rolling for time-based analysis.
modules.intro: The four verbs of the last module prepare the data. Now you answer questions: totals by group, facts from several tables, tables turned sideways, trends over time. Each pandas tool has a SQL twin you have already met, which is the quickest way to learn them: if you understand GROUP BY, then groupby is only new spelling. The labs run the logic in SQL on the ShopLens tables.

topics.title: groupby and aggregation
topics.html:
groupby splits the rows into groups, applies a summary to each group and combines the results, exactly what GROUP BY does. The trick to readable code is named aggregation, which gives each result a clear name.

GROUP BY in both languages
IdeaSQLpandas
Group and countGROUP BY source + COUNT(*).groupby("source").size() or .agg(n=("id","count"))
Sum, mean, min, maxSUM(amount), AVG(amount).agg(total=("amount","sum"))
Distinct countCOUNT(DISTINCT user_id).agg(users=("user_id","nunique"))
Filter groupsHAVING SUM(amount) > 1000.query("revenue > 1000") after agg
Count each categoryGROUP BY x + COUNT(*)df["x"].value_counts()

Orders and revenue by source (SQL)

Join, group and sort. Add HAVING SUM(o.amount) > 5000 to keep only the biggest sources.

Tables: users, orders. Starting query:

SELECT u.source,
       COUNT(*) AS orders,
       SUM(o.amount) AS revenue,
       ROUND(AVG(o.amount), 0) AS avg_order
FROM orders o
JOIN users u ON u.id = o.user_id
GROUP BY u.source
ORDER BY revenue DESC;
Watch out

A count of rows is not a count of customers. After joining orders to users, count counts order rows; use nunique (COUNT DISTINCT) on the customer id to count customers.

Worked example

Read an aggregation

.agg(revenue=("amount", "sum")) on a grouped DataFrame.

  1. The tuple is (column to summarise, function to apply).
  2. The keyword (revenue) names the result column.
  3. as_index=False keeps the group key as a normal column rather than the index.

Answer. Named aggregation makes the output self-explanatory and avoids the multi-level column headers older code produces.

Common mistakes

  • Forgetting as_index=False and then wondering where the group column went.
  • Aggregating a column with mean that should be a sum (revenue versus average order).
  • Counting rows after a join and calling it customers.
Try it yourself: Write pandas for the number of different users per source.

Model answer. users.groupby("source", as_index=False).agg(n=("id", "nunique"))

Check what you just learned

1. Which pandas call is the closest to GROUP BY source with COUNT(*)?
  • df.sort_values
  • df.pivot
  • df.merge
  • df.groupby("source").size() (correct)

groupby plus size counts rows per group.

2. `nunique` is the pandas version of:
  • COUNT(DISTINCT col) (correct)
  • COUNT(*)
  • SUM
  • MAX

It counts distinct values.
keyPoints: groupby is GROUP BY: split, apply a summary, combine.
Use named aggregation for readable output.
Distinguish counting rows from counting distinct entities.

topics.title: merge, concat and the fan-out trap
topics.html:
merge combines two DataFrames on matching columns, the way JOIN does. concat stacks them, the way UNION ALL does.

Joins in both languages
WantSQLpandas
Matching rows onlyINNER JOINa.merge(b, on="id", how="inner")
All rows of the left tableLEFT JOINhow="left"
All rows of bothFULL JOINhow="outer"
Different column namesON a.user_id = b.idleft_on="user_id", right_on="id"
Stack tablesUNION ALLpd.concat([a, b])

The two safety options are among the most valuable in pandas. validate="one_to_many" raises an error if the left key is not unique, which catches a hidden fan-out before it inflates totals. indicator=True adds a column showing which rows matched, so df[df["_merge"] == "left_only"] lists users with no orders (an anti-join).

Users who never ordered (SQL)

The SQL version of a left merge followed by _merge == 'left_only'.

Tables: users, orders. Starting query:

SELECT u.id, u.signup_date, u.source
FROM users u
LEFT JOIN orders o ON o.user_id = u.id
WHERE o.id IS NULL
ORDER BY u.id
LIMIT 10;
Watch out

A merge on a key that is not unique on either side multiplies rows. 3 matching rows on the left times 2 on the right gives 6. Always check len(result) against what you expect, or use validate.

Worked example

Counting after a merge

36 users, 19 orders. A left merge gives how many rows?

  1. Users with no orders give one row each (with missing order columns).
  2. Users with several orders give one row per order.
  3. So the result has more than 36 rows: 36 minus the users with orders, plus all the orders.

Answer. A merge result's length is rarely the same as either input. Predict it, then check.

Common mistakes

  • Using how="inner" and silently dropping unmatched rows.
  • Merging on a column with different types (string versus integer), which matches nothing.
  • Duplicate column names, which pandas suffixes with _x and _y: rename before merging.
Try it yourself: Which option makes pandas raise an error if the left key is duplicated?

Model answer. validate="one_to_many" (or "one_to_one").

Check what you just learned

1. pandas `how="left"` corresponds to:
  • INNER JOIN
  • LEFT JOIN (correct)
  • CROSS JOIN
  • UNION

It keeps every row of the left table.

2. What does `indicator=True` add?
  • A chart
  • An index
  • A column showing which side each row came from (correct)
  • A sort

The _merge column shows both, left_only or right_only.
keyPoints: merge is JOIN (inner, left, outer); concat is UNION ALL.
validate and indicator catch fan-outs and show unmatched rows.
Always predict and check the row count after a merge.

topics.title: Reshaping: pivot_table, melt and crosstab
topics.html:
Data comes in two shapes: long (one row per observation, as in tidy data) and wide (a column per category, good for reading). Analysis prefers long; reports prefer wide. pandas moves between them.

Reshaping tools
DirectionpandasIn a spreadsheet or SQL
Long to widepd.pivot_table(df, index="region", columns="product", values="revenue", aggfunc="sum", fill_value=0, margins=True)A PivotTable, or SUM(CASE WHEN ... END) per column
Wide to longdf.melt(id_vars="product", var_name="month", value_name="sales")Power Query Unpivot, or UNION ALL of columns
Count by two categoriespd.crosstab(df["region"], df["product"])COUNT(*) with two GROUP BY columns

A manual pivot in SQL

Conditional aggregation is how SQL pivots: one SUM(CASE ...) per column. Add a column for the 'pro' plan.

Tables: users, orders. Starting query:

SELECT u.source,
       SUM(CASE WHEN u.plan = 'free' THEN o.amount ELSE 0 END) AS free_revenue,
       SUM(CASE WHEN u.plan = 'pro'  THEN o.amount ELSE 0 END) AS pro_revenue
FROM orders o
JOIN users u ON u.id = o.user_id
GROUP BY u.source;
Worked example

Why melt matters

A sheet has columns product, jan, feb, mar.

  1. Wide data cannot be grouped by month, because month is not a column.
  2. df.melt(id_vars="product", var_name="month", value_name="sales") gives rows (product, month, sales).
  3. Now groupby("month") and a line chart by month both work.

Answer. Melting is the pandas version of Power Query's Unpivot: it makes wide data tidy.

Watch out

pivot_table aggregates: if several rows share an index and column, it applies aggfunc (mean by default!). If you meant to sum revenue, you must say aggfunc="sum". The default mean has fooled many people.

Common mistakes

  • Forgetting aggfunc and getting averages when sums were wanted.
  • Pivoting data that has duplicate index and column pairs without noticing the aggregation.
  • Keeping wide data for analysis, which makes grouping awkward.
Try it yourself: Which function turns columns jan, feb, mar into rows?

Model answer. melt

Check what you just learned

1. Which reshapes wide data into long?
  • pivot_table
  • groupby
  • merge
  • melt (correct)

melt unpivots columns into rows.

2. The default aggfunc of pivot_table is:
  • mean (correct)
  • count
  • sum
  • max

It is mean, so state sum when you want it.
keyPoints: Long data suits analysis; wide data suits reading.
pivot_table goes long to wide, melt goes wide to long; set aggfunc explicitly.
SQL pivots with conditional aggregation.

topics.title: Over time: sort, rank, shift and rolling
topics.html:
Time questions ('how does today compare with yesterday?', 'what is the running total?') are done with ordered, window-style operations. pandas names them differently from SQL, but they are the same ideas as the window functions you learned.

Window ideas in both languages
IdeaSQLpandas
SortORDER BYdf.sort_values("day")
RankRANK() OVER (ORDER BY x DESC)df["x"].rank(ascending=False, method="min")
Previous rowLAG(x)df["x"].shift(1)
Change vs previousx - LAG(x)df["x"].diff() or .pct_change()
Running totalSUM(x) OVER (ORDER BY day)df["x"].cumsum()
Moving averageAVG(x) OVER (... ROWS BETWEEN 2 PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW)df["x"].rolling(3).mean()
Group total on every rowSUM(x) OVER (PARTITION BY g)df.groupby("g")["x"].transform("sum")

A 3-day moving average (SQL)

Seven days of visits. The window averages each day with the two before it. Try a 2-day or 4-day window.

Tables: daily. Starting query:

SELECT day, visits,
       ROUND(AVG(visits) OVER (ORDER BY day
             ROWS BETWEEN 2 PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW), 1) AS avg3
FROM daily;
Result: visits and their 3-day moving average
dayvisitsavg3
03-01100100.0
03-02120110.0
03-0390103.3
03-04140116.7
03-05130120.0
03-06160143.3
03-07150146.7

In pandas the same result is df["visits"].rolling(3).mean(), with one difference worth knowing: pandas leaves the first two values empty (a missing value) because it requires a full window by default. Pass min_periods=1 to match SQL's behaviour of averaging whatever rows exist.

Watch out

These functions assume the data is sorted. shift, cumsum and rolling work on the order of the rows, not on the dates. Sort first (sort_values("day")), and check the dates have no gaps (a missing day makes 'previous row' mean 'two days ago').

Common mistakes

  • Computing a rolling average on unsorted data.
  • Ignoring missing days when 'previous' is meant to be 'yesterday'.
  • Treating the empty first row as if it were zero.
Try it yourself: How do you compute the day-on-day change in visits in pandas?

Model answer. df["visits"].diff() for the absolute change, or df["visits"].pct_change() for the proportional change.

Check what you just learned

1. `df["x"].shift(1)` is the pandas version of:
  • LEAD
  • LAG(x) (correct)
  • SUM
  • RANK

It moves values down one row, giving the previous value.

2. Before using rolling or shift you should:
  • Convert to text
  • Delete the index
  • Sort by the time column (correct)
  • Drop all columns

They work on row order.

Key terms: flip and sort

groupby
Split rows into groups and summarise each.
Named aggregation
agg(name=(column, function)).
merge
pandas join.
validate
A merge option that checks key uniqueness.
pivot_table / melt
Long to wide / wide to long.
rolling
A moving window calculation.
shift
Move values down to get the previous row.
keyPoints: pandas shift, diff, cumsum, rolling and rank mirror SQL's LAG, running SUM, moving AVG and RANK.
Sort first, and check for missing days.
rolling leaves the first rows empty unless min_periods is set.

modules.title: SQL for analysts: funnels, cohorts and segments
modules.summary: Use SQL for the questions product and marketing teams ask every week: where users drop off, who comes back, and which customers matter most.
modules.outcome: You can build a conversion funnel, a cohort retention table and an RFM segmentation, and you can find and remove duplicate records with window functions.
modules.intro: Three analyses appear in nearly every analytics job: the funnel (how many users get from each step to the next), retention (how many come back), and segmentation (who are the best customers). All three are a few lines of SQL once you see the pattern, and all rely on tools you already have: COUNT DISTINCT, window functions and CASE. This module teaches the patterns with tiny tables you can check by eye, then applies them to the ShopLens shop data in the labs.

topics.title: Funnels: where do users drop off?
topics.html:
A funnel counts how many users reach each step of a journey: visit, sign up, add to cart, purchase. The percentage lost at each step shows where to focus.

Six users and the steps they reached
UserSteps reached
1visit, signup, cart, purchase
2visit, signup, cart
3visit, signup
4visit
5visit, signup, cart, purchase
6visit, signup

Count users at each step

COUNT(DISTINCT user_id) counts each user once per step, even if they repeated it. Run it, then add the conversion columns below.

Tables: steps. Starting query:

SELECT step, COUNT(DISTINCT user_id) AS users
FROM steps
GROUP BY step;

Counts alone do not show the conversion. Put the steps in order with a number, then compare each row with the first (overall conversion) and the one before (step conversion) using window functions:

Result
stepuserspct_of_visitspct_of_previous
visit6100.0NULL
signup583.383.3
cart350.060.0
purchase233.366.7
Worked example

Reading the funnel

Of six visitors, two buy: an overall conversion of 33.3%.

  1. The biggest step loss in percentage terms is between signup and cart: 60% continue, so 40% leave.
  2. From cart to purchase, 66.7% continue, and the biggest absolute loss is signup to cart (two users).
  3. Focus the next experiment on getting signed-up users to add something to the cart.

Answer. A funnel turns 'conversion is low' into 'this step is where users leave'.

Watch out

Count distinct users, not events. A user who visits ten times is one user in the funnel. COUNT(*) would count ten, and a funnel where later steps exceed earlier ones is a sign you counted events.

Common mistakes

  • Counting events instead of distinct users.
  • Not restricting to a time window, so old users inflate a recent funnel.
  • Treating steps as strictly ordered when some users skip steps; decide the rule and state it.
Try it yourself: Which window function gives the previous step's user count?

Model answer. LAG(users) OVER (ORDER BY n)

Check what you just learned

1. Why COUNT(DISTINCT user_id) in a funnel?
  • It is faster
  • To sort
  • SQL requires it
  • A user who repeats a step must count once (correct)

Funnels count people, not events.

2. 'pct_of_previous' uses:
  • LAG (correct)
  • FIRST_VALUE
  • NTILE
  • UNION

LAG supplies the previous step's count.
keyPoints: A funnel counts distinct users who reached each step.
Compare each step with the top (overall) and with the previous step (step conversion).
Count distinct users, within a defined time window.

topics.title: Cohorts and retention
topics.html:
A cohort is a group of users who share a starting point, such as the month they signed up. Retention asks what share of each cohort is still active one month later, two months later, and so on. It answers 'are we keeping customers?', which averages across all users cannot, because new users hide the leavers.

Activity log: user, signup month, and the months they were active
UserSignupActive in
AJanJan, Feb, Mar
BJanJan, Feb
CJanJan
DFebFeb, Mar
EFebFeb

Retention by cohort

Month offset 0 is the signup month (always 100%). Offset 1 is the next month. Change ROUND(...) or add offset 2 only.

Tables: activity. Starting query:

WITH size AS (
  SELECT signup_m, COUNT(DISTINCT user_id) AS n
  FROM activity GROUP BY signup_m
)
SELECT a.signup_m AS cohort,
       a.active_m - a.signup_m AS month_offset,
       COUNT(DISTINCT a.user_id) AS active,
       ROUND(100.0 * COUNT(DISTINCT a.user_id) / MAX(s.n), 0) AS pct
FROM activity a
JOIN size s ON s.signup_m = a.signup_m
GROUP BY a.signup_m, a.active_m - a.signup_m
ORDER BY cohort, month_offset;
Result
cohortmonth offsetactivepct
Jan03100
Jan1267
Jan2133
Feb02100
Feb1150
Worked example

Reading the table

January's cohort: 100%, 67%, 33%. February's: 100%, 50%.

  1. Each row is one cohort, each column a month since signup.
  2. January lost a third of users after one month, then another third.
  3. February kept 50% after one month, worse than January's 67%: a warning that newer users are churning faster.

Answer. Comparing cohorts at the same age is the point. Comparing January's month 2 with February's month 1 would mislead.

Watch out

The latest cohorts are incomplete: a user who signed up last week has had no chance to return next month. Show only offsets that the cohort has had time to reach, or the right edge of the table will look like falling retention when it is only missing data.

Common mistakes

  • Defining 'active' differently for each cohort.
  • Comparing cohorts at different ages.
  • Using calendar months without checking that every month in the data is complete.
Try it yourself: What does month offset 0 always equal?

Model answer. 100% of the cohort, because users are active in their signup month by definition (if active means 'signed up').

Check what you just learned

1. Why use cohorts rather than overall retention?
  • They are faster
  • New users hide the loss of old users in an overall average (correct)
  • SQL requires it
  • They need no dates

Cohorts compare like with like.

2. Month offset is:
  • The signup month
  • The number of users
  • The active month minus the signup month (correct)
  • The cohort size

It measures time since signup.
keyPoints: A cohort is a group sharing a starting point; retention is the share still active after n periods.
Compute the offset as active period minus cohort period, and divide by the cohort size.
Compare cohorts at the same age and hide incomplete cells.

topics.title: Segmentation: RFM and ranking customers
topics.html:
Not all customers are equal. RFM scores each customer on three behaviours: Recency (how long since the last order), Frequency (how many orders) and Monetary value (how much they spent). Together they separate loyal, lapsing and one-time customers.

Five customers' orders, as of 1 July 2025
CustomerOrdersLast orderTotal spent
P225 June800
Q12 May1,200
R315 May750
S128 June900
T115 January100

Compute recency, frequency and monetary

DATEDIFF gives days since the last order. Add a segment with CASE: for example VIP when frequency >= 2.

Tables: buys. Starting query:

SELECT customer,
       DATEDIFF('2025-07-01', MAX(order_date)) AS recency_days,
       COUNT(*) AS frequency,
       SUM(amount) AS monetary
FROM buys
GROUP BY customer
ORDER BY customer;

Scores turn each measure into a rank. NTILE(n) splits customers into n equal-sized groups by a measure: NTILE(3) OVER (ORDER BY monetary DESC) gives 1 to the top third, 2 to the middle third, 3 to the bottom third. Combining the three scores gives segments such as 'champions' (recent, frequent, high spend) and 'at risk' (valuable but not seen for a long time).

A simple segment rule set
SegmentRule (example)Action
ChampionRecent (within 30 days) and 2+ ordersReward, ask for referrals
PromisingRecent, 1 orderEncourage a second order
At riskNot seen for 60+ days but spent 1,000+Win-back offer
LapsedNot seen for 90+ days, low spendLow-cost reminder or leave
Worked example

Reading the RFM table

Customer Q spent 1,200 on one order 60 days ago. Customer S spent 900, 3 days ago.

  1. Q has the highest spend but is drifting away: 60 days of silence.
  2. S is recent but has ordered only once.
  3. Both matter for different reasons: Q for a win-back message, S for a second-order nudge.

Answer. Segmentation turns one list of customers into different next actions, which is the entire point.

Watch out

Cut-offs such as '60 days' are choices, not facts. Pick them from your business's normal buying rhythm (a grocery shop and a car dealer differ), and write them down.

Common mistakes

  • Using today's date inside the query, so the results change every day. Use a fixed 'as of' date.
  • Equal-sized NTILE groups on very few customers, which splits ties arbitrarily.
  • Treating segments as permanent labels rather than a snapshot.
Try it yourself: What does NTILE(4) OVER (ORDER BY spend DESC) return for the biggest spender?

Model answer. 1: the top quartile.

Check what you just learned

1. Recency in RFM measures:
  • How much spent
  • Customer age
  • Number of orders
  • Days since the last order (correct)

R is for recency.

2. NTILE(3) splits rows into:
  • Three equal-sized groups by order (correct)
  • Three columns
  • Three tables
  • Three filters

Each group has about a third of the rows.
keyPoints: RFM measures recency, frequency and monetary value per customer.
NTILE and CASE turn measures into scores and segments.
Use a fixed as-of date and document your cut-offs.

topics.title: Quality checks: duplicates, joins and sanity tests
topics.html:
Every metric in this module can be wrong if the data is. Build checks into the analysis, not after it.

Keep the latest record for each email

ROW_NUMBER numbers the records for each email, newest first; rn = 1 keeps the latest. Change DESC to ASC to keep the oldest.

Tables: contacts. Starting query:

SELECT id, email, updated_at
FROM (
  SELECT id, email, updated_at,
         ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY email
                            ORDER BY updated_at DESC) AS rn
  FROM contacts
) t
WHERE rn = 1
ORDER BY id;

This deduplication pattern, a window function that numbers records inside each group and a filter on the first, is the standard answer to 'keep one row per key'. It beats DISTINCT, which only removes rows identical in every column, so it fails when two records for the same person have different ids or timestamps.

Sanity checks to run on any analysis
CheckHowWhat it catches
Row counts at each stepSELECT COUNT(*) after each join or filterFan-outs and accidental filters
Totals reconcileCompare to a known figureMissing or double-counted data
Keys are uniqueCOUNT(*) versus COUNT(DISTINCT id)Duplicate records
Dates are in rangeMIN and MAX of every date columnTest data and typos
No impossible valuesNegative quantities, future datesData entry errors
Cohorts add upSum of cohort sizes = total usersUsers lost in a join
Worked example

A check that saved a report

A revenue query returned 30,600 and the finance system said 24,100.

  1. Check keys: COUNT(*) was larger than COUNT(DISTINCT order_id). The join to a promotions table had repeated orders.
  2. Fix: aggregate promotions to one row per order before joining.
  3. Re-run: 24,100. It now reconciles.

Answer. Reconciling to a trusted total is the most powerful single check.

Watch out

A query that runs without error is not a query that is right. Plausible-looking wrong answers are the most dangerous kind.

Common mistakes

  • Trusting a result because it looks reasonable.
  • Using DISTINCT to hide a join problem instead of fixing it.
  • Never comparing with a second source.
Try it yourself: Which pattern keeps only the latest record for each customer?

Model answer. ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY customer ORDER BY updated_at DESC) and filter rn = 1.

Check what you just learned

1. Why can DISTINCT fail to remove duplicates?
  • It is slow
  • It only removes rows identical in every column (correct)
  • It sorts
  • It needs an index

A different id or timestamp makes rows distinct.

2. The strongest single sanity check is to:
  • Count columns
  • Sort the result
  • Reconcile to a trusted total (correct)
  • Add LIMIT

A known figure exposes errors.

Key terms: flip and sort

Funnel
Counts of users reaching each step.
Cohort
Users who share a starting point.
Retention
The share of a cohort still active after n periods.
RFM
Recency, frequency, monetary value.
NTILE
Splits ordered rows into equal groups.
Deduplicate
Keep one row per key.
Reconcile
Compare a result with a trusted total.
keyPoints: ROW_NUMBER with PARTITION BY and a filter on rn = 1 keeps one row per key.
Check row counts, uniqueness, date ranges and reconcile to a known total.
Do not use DISTINCT to hide problems.

modules.title: Explore, visualise and reason with statistics
modules.summary: Explore a dataset systematically, choose and draw the right chart, and use basic statistics to say how sure you are.
modules.outcome: You can follow an exploratory data analysis checklist, draw histograms, bar, line and scatter charts with matplotlib and seaborn, compute a confidence interval, and spot bias, confounding and Simpson's paradox.
modules.intro: Exploratory data analysis (EDA) is the habit of looking at the data from several angles before concluding anything: its shape, its gaps, its extremes, and how its parts relate. Charts make patterns visible that tables hide, and a little statistics tells you how much to trust what you see. This module gives you a checklist, the plotting code, and the reasoning habits that keep you honest. As before, the Python is for a notebook; the SQL and sheet-style practice run here.

topics.title: An EDA checklist
topics.html:
A checklist stops you from skipping the boring steps that catch the biggest errors.

Seven questions to ask of every new dataset

  • Size and grain: how many rows, and what does one row represent?
  • Types: are dates dates and numbers numbers?
  • Missingness: where are the gaps and are they random?
  • Distributions: what does each numeric column look like?
  • Categories: how many values, any typos?
  • Extremes: what are the largest and smallest values, and are they real?
  • Relationships: which columns move together?
Worked example

The grain question

A table has one row per order item. Someone asks for 'orders per customer'.

  1. COUNT(*) counts items, not orders.
  2. Count distinct order ids instead.
  3. Say what one row is before you count it.

Answer. Most counting mistakes are grain mistakes. Always state what a row represents.

Rows, orders and customers are three different counts

Same table, three counts. Change COUNT(DISTINCT ...) to see how each differs.

Tables: orders. Starting query:

SELECT COUNT(*) AS rows_in_table,
       COUNT(DISTINCT id) AS orders,
       COUNT(DISTINCT user_id) AS customers,
       ROUND(1.0 * COUNT(*) / COUNT(DISTINCT user_id), 2) AS orders_per_customer
FROM orders;
Watch out

The Python code in this course does not run in this browser. Copy it into a free notebook (Google Colab needs nothing installed) to try it. The SQL windows and the labs do run here.

Tip

Write your EDA findings in the notebook as you go: 'three cities missing', 'order 90,000 looks like a typo'. Future you, and your reviewer, will thank you.

Common mistakes

  • Computing statistics before looking at distributions.
  • Trusting averages without looking at the extremes.
  • Not stating the grain of the table.
Try it yourself: What is the grain of an orders table with one row per order line?

Model answer. One row per order line (item). Count distinct order ids to count orders.

Check what you just learned

1. What does 'grain' mean?
  • Column width
  • The data type
  • The file size
  • What one row of the table represents (correct)

It determines what counting means.

2. Why look at the largest rows?
  • To find errors or special cases (correct)
  • Style
  • To sort
  • To rename

Extremes are often typos or the most important cases.
keyPoints: Ask size and grain, types, gaps, distributions, categories, extremes and relationships.
Look at actual extreme rows, not just summaries.
State what one row represents before you count.

topics.title: Charts that tell the truth
topics.html:
Four charts cover most analysis: histogram, bar, line and scatter. Pick by the question.

Question to chart
QuestionChartpandas / seaborn
How are values distributed?Histogram or box plotdf["amount"].plot(kind="hist", bins=10); sns.boxplot(x="source", y="amount", data=df)
How do categories compare?Bar chart, sorteddf.groupby("source")["amount"].sum().sort_values().plot(kind="barh")
How does a measure change over time?Line chartmonthly.plot(x="month", y="revenue")
Are two numbers related?Scatter plotsns.scatterplot(x="visits", y="orders", data=df)
Which columns correlate?Heatmapsns.heatmap(df.corr(numeric_only=True), annot=True)

Rules for honest charts

  • Bars start at zero; lines may not.
  • Sort bars by value unless the categories have a natural order.
  • Label axes and units; title with the finding, not the topic.
  • One message per chart; use colour to highlight, not to decorate.
  • Avoid pie charts with many slices, and 3D effects altogether.
Watch out

The default chart is rarely the finished chart. Add a title, label the axes, sort the bars and remove clutter before showing anyone.

Common mistakes

  • A bar chart with a truncated axis.
  • Plotting too many categories (use the top 10 and 'Other').
  • Using a line chart for unordered categories.
Try it yourself: Which chart suits 'how are order values spread?'

Model answer. A histogram (or a box plot to compare groups).

Check what you just learned

1. Which chart shows the distribution of one numeric column?
  • Pie
  • Histogram (correct)
  • Line
  • Map

A histogram counts values per bin.

2. A good chart title:
  • Names the topic
  • Is omitted
  • States the finding (correct)
  • Is long

Tell the reader what to see.
keyPoints: Histogram for distribution, bar for comparison, line for time, scatter for relationships.
Bars start at zero; sort, label and title with the finding.
One message per chart.

topics.title: Samples, uncertainty and confidence intervals
topics.html:
Almost every dataset is a sample of something larger: this month's customers stand for all customers; 200 survey answers stand for a population. A sample average is an estimate, and different samples would give different averages. The standard error measures how much a sample mean typically wobbles.

Formula · Standard error and a 95% confidence interval

SE = s ÷ √n CI ≈ mean ± 1.96 × SE

s is the sample standard deviation and n the sample size. The factor 1.96 gives about 95% coverage for a large enough sample of roughly bell-shaped data.

Worked example

A worked interval

A sample of 100 orders has an average of ₹50 and a standard deviation of ₹20.

  1. SE = 20 ÷ √100 = 20 ÷ 10 = 2.
  2. 1.96 × 2 = 3.92.
  3. 95% interval: 50 ± 3.92, so about ₹46.1 to ₹53.9.

Answer. We are roughly 95% confident that the true average order is between about ₹46 and ₹54.

How sample size shrinks the margin of error

The spread stays at ₹20. See how the margin shrinks as n grows (it falls with the square root, so quadrupling n halves it).

Adjust Sample size, Standard deviation (₹) and see Standard error, 95% margin of error (±) change.

Watch out

A confidence interval describes the uncertainty from sampling. It does not cover bias (a sample that is not representative) or mistakes in the data. A precise answer to the wrong question is still wrong.

Common mistakes

  • Reporting an average with no sense of how many rows it rests on.
  • Reading a 95% interval as 'there is a 95% chance this single result is right'.
  • Forgetting that small groups have wide intervals: do not compare a 12-customer city with a 1,200-customer one at face value.
Try it yourself: If you quadruple the sample size, what happens to the margin of error?

Model answer. It halves, because it falls with the square root of n.

Check what you just learned

1. Margin of error when s = 20 and n = 100 (95%) is about:
  • ±0.4
  • ±1.96
  • ±20
  • ±3.9 (correct)

1.96 × 20 ÷ 10 = 3.92.

2. Quadrupling the sample size does what to the margin of error?
  • Halves it (correct)
  • Doubles it
  • Leaves it
  • Removes it

It depends on the square root of n.
keyPoints: SE = s ÷ √n; a 95% interval is about mean ± 1.96 × SE.
Bigger samples give narrower intervals, with diminishing returns.
Intervals cover sampling noise, not bias or data errors.

topics.title: Bias, confounding and Simpson's paradox
topics.html:
Statistics can tell you how precise a number is. It cannot tell you whether the number answers your question. These traps do the most damage.

Common traps
TrapWhat happensExample
Selection biasThe data is not representative of the group you care aboutSurveying only customers who stayed; those who left never answer
Survivorship biasOnly successes appear in the dataStudying the habits of successful startups and ignoring those that failed
ConfoundingA hidden factor drives both variablesIce cream sales and drownings both rise in summer
Simpson's paradoxA trend reverses when groups are combinedSee below
Cherry-pickingReporting only the favourable resultShowing the one month the campaign worked
Worked example

Simpson's paradox

Two ad campaigns. Campaign A converts better for both new and returning customers, yet B looks better overall.

  1. Campaign A: new customers 20 of 200 (10.0%), returning customers 15 of 30 (50.0%). Overall 35 of 230 (15.2%).
  2. Campaign B: new customers 3 of 40 (7.5%), returning customers 130 of 300 (43.3%). Overall 133 of 340 (39.1%).
  3. A wins in both groups, but B wins overall because 88% of B's audience was returning customers, who convert far more, while most of A's audience was new.

Answer. When groups differ in size and behaviour, compare within groups first, and ask why the mix differs.

Watch out

Correlation is not causation. Establishing cause needs a controlled experiment (an A/B test with random assignment) or careful design. Observational data can suggest causes; it rarely proves them.

Questions that protect you

  • Who is not in this data, and would they answer differently?
  • What else could explain this pattern?
  • Does the result hold within each group, not only overall?
  • Would I report this if the result were the opposite?
  • How many comparisons did I make? The more you test, the more chance patterns appear.

Common mistakes

  • Comparing overall rates when group mixes differ.
  • Looking at many cuts of the data and reporting the one that 'worked'.
  • Treating a correlation in observational data as a recommendation.
Try it yourself: Why does studying only successful companies mislead?

Model answer. Failed companies with the same habits are missing, so you cannot tell whether the habits helped (survivorship bias).

Check what you just learned

1. Studying only the companies that survived is:
  • Selection of the best data
  • Survivorship bias (correct)
  • Random sampling
  • A confidence interval

The failures are missing.

2. When overall results conflict with results inside each group, you should:
  • Ignore the groups
  • Average everything
  • Look at group mix and compare within groups (correct)
  • Delete the groups

The mix of groups explains the reversal.

Key terms: flip and sort

EDA
Exploratory data analysis: looking before concluding.
Grain
What one row represents.
Standard error
How much a sample mean wobbles: s ÷ √n.
Confidence interval
A range of plausible values for the true figure.
Selection bias
A sample that does not represent the group of interest.
Confounder
A hidden factor driving two variables.
Simpson's paradox
A trend that reverses when groups are combined.
keyPoints: Check who is missing from the data (selection and survivorship bias).
Compare within groups before combining them; Simpson's paradox is common when group mixes differ.
Observational correlation is not causation; test with experiments where possible.

topics.title: A SQL-to-pandas pipeline
topics.html:
Real projects chain the tools: SQL extracts a small, well-defined table; pandas cleans and analyses it; a chart or a report presents it.

Watch out

Never build a query by pasting user input into a string. "... WHERE city = '" + city + "'" lets a malicious value change your query (SQL injection). Pass values as parameters (? or %s), as in the example, and the database treats them purely as data. The Python code in this course does not run in this browser. Copy it into a free notebook (Google Colab needs nothing installed) to try it. The SQL windows and the labs do run here.

Choosing where to do each step
StepDo it in SQL whenDo it in pandas when
FilteringThe table is largeThe data is already small and in memory
AggregatingYou can reduce millions of rows to hundredsYou need many different cuts of a small table
JoiningThe tables live in the same databaseOne table is a local file
Statistics, models, chartsNeverAlways
Worked example

Why the date filter lives in SQL

Last year's orders are 2 million rows, but you need 2025 only.

  1. Filter with WHERE order_date >= '2025-01-01' in the query.
  2. Only the matching rows travel to your notebook.
  3. Memory stays small and the notebook stays fast.

Answer. Push filters and aggregates to the database; pull results into pandas.

Common mistakes

  • SELECT * from a huge table, then filtering in Python.
  • String-pasting values into SQL.
  • Doing statistics in SQL because it is possible, when pandas is clearer.
Try it yourself: How do you pass a date safely into pd.read_sql?

Model answer. Use a parameter placeholder in the SQL and pass params=[value].

Check what you just learned

1. What is SQL injection?
  • A fast query
  • A chart
  • A join type
  • Malicious input changing the meaning of a query built by string pasting (correct)

Parameters prevent it.

2. Which step belongs in the database?
  • Filtering a huge table (correct)
  • Charts
  • Writing the memo
  • Colouring

Reduce the data before moving it.
keyPoints: Extract small, aggregated tables with SQL; analyse and chart in pandas.
Use query parameters, never string pasting, to avoid SQL injection.
Push filters and aggregates to the database.

topics.title: Reproducible analysis
topics.html:
Reproducible means someone else (or you in six months) can re-run the work and get the same answer, and understand how. It is the difference between an analysis and a one-off.

Habits that make work reproducible

  • Run top to bottom: restart the notebook and run all cells before sharing; if it fails, fix it.
  • No hidden state: do not depend on a variable defined in a deleted cell.
  • Put settings at the top: dates, file paths, thresholds, so one change updates everything.
  • Turn repeated steps into functions with names that say what they do.
  • Write down the definitions: what 'active user' means, which statuses count as revenue.
  • Record the data source and extract date.
  • Use version control (Git) to track changes, with clear commit messages.
Git in four commands
CommandWhat it does
git initStart tracking a folder
git add notebook.ipynbChoose what goes in the next snapshot
git commit -m "Add retention analysis"Save a snapshot with a message
git logSee the history
Worked example

A data dictionary line

For each column, write a line that someone new can understand.

  1. signup_date: date the user created an account, in the shop's local time, ISO format.
  2. source: where the user came from; one of organic, ads, referral.
  3. amount: order value in rupees including GST; refunds are separate rows with negative amounts.

Answer. Definitions prevent the most common argument in analytics: two people using the same word for different things.

Watch out

Never commit passwords, API keys or personal data to a repository, even a private one. Keep credentials in environment variables or a secrets manager.

Common mistakes

  • Sharing a notebook that only works if cells are run in a particular order.
  • Hard-coding values in the middle of an analysis.
  • Not saving the query that produced the data.

Check what you just learned

1. A reproducible notebook is one that:
  • Has many colours
  • Runs from top to bottom after a restart (correct)
  • Uses only SQL
  • Has no text

Order and hidden state are the usual problems.

2. Which should never go into a Git repository?
  • Code
  • A README
  • Passwords and API keys (correct)
  • A data dictionary

Secrets must be kept out.
keyPoints: A reproducible analysis re-runs top to bottom and documents its definitions and sources.
Put settings at the top, use functions, add sanity checks.
Use version control and never commit secrets or personal data.

topics.title: Privacy, ethics and communicating results
topics.html:
Analysts often handle information about real people. Using it responsibly is part of the job, and the law increasingly requires it. (This is general guidance, not legal advice; the course on data privacy covers the laws in more depth.)

Working responsibly with personal data
PrincipleIn practice
Collect and use only what you needDo you need names and phone numbers to analyse retention? Often an anonymous id is enough
Remove identifiers earlyReplace names and contact details with ids before analysis
Limit accessShare the least detail with the fewest people
Protect small groupsDo not publish a result for a group of two or three people: it can identify them
Be honest about purposeUse data only for the reason people agreed to; laws such as India's DPDP Act 2023 and the EU's GDPR set rules on consent and purpose

Communicating is the last mile. Lead with the answer, give two or three pieces of evidence, state the limits, and recommend an action, exactly the shape you used in the SQL course's memo.

A one-page structure
PartContent
HeadlineThe finding, in a sentence
EvidenceTwo or three numbers or charts, with their definitions
LimitsWhat the data does not show; sample size; missing groups
RecommendationWhat to do, who, by when
AppendixDefinitions, queries, data source and date
Worked example

A finding written well

Retention analysis for January to March signups.

  1. Headline: One in two February signups is gone after a month, worse than January's one in three.
  2. Evidence: month-1 retention was 67% for January and 50% for February in this course's small example cohorts; with real data, always show the cohort sizes beside the percentages.
  3. Limit: the March cohort is incomplete, so it is not shown.
  4. Recommendation: review the February onboarding emails before the next campaign.

Answer. In four lines the reader knows what happened, how sure to be, and what to do.

Watch out

Resist overstating. 'Retention fell' is a fact; 'the new homepage caused retention to fall' is a claim that needs evidence. Say which you are making.

Common mistakes

  • Sharing data with personal details when ids would do.
  • Publishing results for tiny groups.
  • A conclusion without a limit.
Try it yourself: Which is better for a retention analysis: names and phone numbers, or anonymous ids?

Model answer. Anonymous ids: the analysis does not need to know who people are, so do not use that information.

Check what you just learned

1. Before analysing retention you should:
  • Add more personal data
  • Remove all dates
  • Publish the raw data
  • Replace names with anonymous ids (correct)

Minimise identifying information.

2. A strong finding includes:
  • The answer, evidence, limits and a recommendation (correct)
  • Only a chart
  • Only the method
  • A long story

Decision makers need all four.

Key terms: flip and sort

Pipeline
SQL extract, pandas analysis, report.
SQL injection
Malicious input altering a pasted-together query.
Parameter
A value passed separately from the SQL text.
Reproducible
Re-runnable by someone else with the same result.
Data dictionary
Definitions for each column.
Anonymisation
Removing identifying details.
keyPoints: Use only the personal data you need; remove identifiers early; protect small groups.
Laws such as the DPDP Act 2023 and GDPR set rules; follow your organisation's policy.
Lead with the finding; state the limits and a specific recommendation.
